nodes.name: Three motivations for missing value reconstruction
nodes.statement: Missing value reconstruction is interesting in at least three different senses. Firstly, it can be used to cope with data that really has missing values. Secondly, reconstruction performance of artificially missing values can be used as a measure of performance in unsupervised learning \citep{raiko2001missing}. Thirdly, reconstruction of artificially missing values can be used as a training criterion \citep{brakel2013training,goodfellow2013multi,uria2014deep}. While traditional RNN training criterions correspond to one-step prediction, training to reconstruct longer gaps can push the model towards concentrating on longer-term predictions. Note that the one-step prediction criterion is typically used even in approaches that otherwise concentrate on modelling long-term dependencies \citep[see e.g.][]{mikolov2014learning,koutnik2014clockwork}.
nodes.statement_short: Missing-value reconstruction matters as data repair, as an unsupervised performance measure, and as a training criterion pushing models toward long-term prediction.

nodes.name: Intractability of smoothing inference in unidirectional RNNs
nodes.statement: When using unidirectional RNNs as generative models, it is straightforward to draw samples from the model in sequential order. However, inference is not trivial in smoothing tasks, where we want to evaluate probabilities for missing values in the middle of a time series. For discrete data, inference with gap sizes of one is feasible - however, inference with larger gap sizes becomes exponentially more expensive. Even sampling can be exponentially expensive with respect to the gap size.
nodes.statement_short: Sampling and inference for a gap in the middle of a sequence cost exponentially in the gap size for a unidirectional RNN.
assumptions: When using unidirectional RNNs as generative models
we want to evaluate probabilities for missing values in the middle of a time series
conclusions: inference is not trivial in smoothing tasks
inference with larger gap sizes becomes exponentially more expensive
Even sampling can be exponentially expensive with respect to the gap size.

nodes.name: Contribution of this paper
nodes.statement: In this paper, we compare different methods of using RNNs to infer missing values for binary time series data. We evaluate the performance of two generative models that rely on bidirectional RNNs, and compare them to inference using a unidirectional RNN. The proposed methods are very favourable in terms of scalability.
nodes.statement_short: The paper compares two bidirectional-RNN generative models against unidirectional-RNN inference for missing binary time series values.

nodes.name: Recurrent neural network (RNN)
nodes.statement: Recurrent neural networks \citep{rumelhart1986learning,haykin2009neural} can be seen as extensions of the standard feedforward multilayer perceptron networks, where the inputs and outputs are sequences instead of individual observations. Let us denote the input to a recurrent neural network by $\mathbf{X} = \left\lbrace \mathbf{x}_t \right\rbrace$ where $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is an input vector for each time step $t$. Let us further denote the output as $\mathbf{Y} = \left\lbrace \mathbf{y}_t \right\rbrace$ where $\mathbf{y}_t \in \mathbb{R}^M$ is an output vector for each time step $t$. Our goal is to model the distribution $P \left( \mathbf{Y} | \mathbf{X} \right)$. Although RNNs map input sequences to output sequences, we can use them in an unsupervised manner by letting the RNN predict the next input. We can do so by setting $\mathbf{Y} = \left\lbrace \mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{x}_{t+1} \right\rbrace$.
nodes.statement_short: An RNN maps an input sequence $\mathbf{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_t\}$ to an output sequence $\mathbf{Y}=\{\mathbf{y}_t\}$; setting $\mathbf{y}_t=\mathbf{x}_{t+1}$ makes it unsupervised.
nodes.genus: extensions of the standard feedforward multilayer perceptron networks
differentia: where the inputs and outputs are sequences instead of individual observations

nodes.name: Unidirectional RNN output distribution
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^t\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y} \mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{y} \right) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The output distribution at time $t$ is a nonlinearity $\phi$ applied to an affine map of the hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$.

nodes.name: Unidirectional RNN hidden state recursion
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \mathbf{h}_t = \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h} \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h} \right) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The hidden state is a $\tanh$ of the previous hidden state plus the current input, both affinely mapped.

nodes.name: Bidirectional recurrent neural network (BRNN)
nodes.statement: Bidirectional RNNs (BRNN) \citep{schuster1997bidirectional,baldi1999exploiting} extend the unidirectional RNN by introducing a second hidden layer, where the hidden to hidden connections flow in opposite temporal order. The model is therefore able to exploit information both from the past and the future.
nodes.statement_short: A BRNN adds a second hidden layer whose recurrent connections run backwards in time, so predictions may use both past and future.
differentia: introducing a second hidden layer, where the hidden to hidden connections flow in opposite temporal order

nodes.name: Traditional BRNN output distribution
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t}\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}_{t}^\mathrm{f} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}_{t}^\mathrm{b} + \mathbf{b}_y \right), \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The conventional BRNN output at $t$ combines the forward and backward hidden states taken at time $t$ itself.

nodes.name: Proposed BRNN output distribution
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} P\left(\mathbf{y}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t}\right) = \mathrm{\phi} \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}_{t-1}^\mathrm{f} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{y}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}_{t+1}^\mathrm{b} + \mathbf{b}_y \right) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The proposed BRNN output at $t$ uses $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^\mathrm{f}$ and $\mathbf{h}_{t+1}^\mathrm{b}$, so $\mathbf{y}_t$ never sees $\mathbf{x}_t$.

nodes.name: BRNN forward and backward hidden state recursions
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \mathbf{h}_t^\mathrm{f} &= \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{h}^\mathrm{f} _{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x}^\mathrm{f} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{f} \right) \\ \mathbf{h}_t^\mathrm{b} &= \tanh \left( \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{h}^\mathrm{b}_{t+1} + \mathbf{W}_\mathrm{x}^\mathrm{b} \mathbf{x}_{t} + \mathbf{b}_\mathrm{h}^\mathrm{b} \right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Forward and backward hidden states each follow a $\tanh$ recursion with their own untied weights.

nodes.name: Acyclicity and self-exclusion of the proposed BRNN
nodes.statement: Note that the connections are acyclic. Note also that in the proposed formulation, $\mathbf{y}_{t}$ does not get information from $\mathbf{x}_{t}$. We can therefore use the model in an unsupervised manner to predict one time step given all other time steps in the input sequence simply by setting $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Because the graph is acyclic and $\mathbf{y}_t$ ignores $\mathbf{x}_t$, setting $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}$ gives an unsupervised leave-one-out predictor.

nodes.name: Unidirectional joint distribution of a sequence
nodes.statement: \begin{align} P_{\mathrm{unidirectional}}(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_{t=1}^T P(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1}). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The unidirectional RNN's joint sequence distribution factorizes as a product of one-step-ahead conditionals.

nodes.name: Generative Stochastic Networks (GSN)
nodes.statement: Generative Stochastic Networks (GSN) \citep{bengio2013generalized} use a denoising auto-encoder to estimate the data distribution as the asymptotic distribution of the Markov chain that alternates between corruption and denoising. The resulting distribution is thus defined only implicitly, and cannot be written analytically.
nodes.statement_short: GSNs define the data distribution implicitly as the asymptotic distribution of a corrupt-then-denoise Markov chain.
differentia: estimate the data distribution as the asymptotic distribution of the Markov chain that alternates between corruption and denoising

nodes.name: A BRNN feedforward pass implements GSN corruption and denoising
nodes.statement: We can define a corruption function that masks $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ as missing, and a denoising function that reconstructs it from the others. It turns out that one feedforward pass of the BRNN does exactly that.
nodes.statement_short: Masking $\mathbf{x}_t$ and reconstructing it from the rest is exactly what one forward pass of the BRNN computes.
assumptions: We can define a corruption function that masks $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ as missing, and a denoising function that reconstructs it from the others
conclusions: one feedforward pass of the BRNN does exactly that

nodes.name: GSN interpretation of the BRNN joint distribution
nodes.statement: Our first probabilistic interpretation is thus that the joint distribution defined by a BRNN is the asymptotic distribution of a process that replaces one observation vector $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ at a time in $\mathbf{X}$ by sampling it from $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$. In practice, we will start from a random initialization and use Gibbs sampling.
nodes.statement_short: Interpret the BRNN joint law as the stationary distribution of Gibbs resampling one $\mathbf{x}_t$ at a time from $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}$.
nodes.genus: the asymptotic distribution of a process
differentia: replaces one observation vector $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ at a time in $\mathbf{X}$ by sampling it from $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$

nodes.name: Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimator (NADE)
nodes.statement: The Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimator (NADE) \citep{uria2014deep} defines a probabilistic model by reconstructing missing components of a vector one at a time in a random order, starting from a fully unobserved vector. Each reconstruction is given by an auto-encoder network that takes as input the observations so far and an auxiliary mask vector that indicates which values are missing.
nodes.statement_short: NADE builds a probabilistic model by reconstructing a vector's components one at a time in random order from a fully unobserved start.
differentia: reconstructing missing components of a vector one at a time in a random order, starting from a fully unobserved vector
Each reconstruction is given by an auto-encoder network that takes as input the observations so far and an auxiliary mask vector that indicates which values are missing

nodes.name: NADE interpretation of the BRNN for time series
nodes.statement: We extend the same idea for time series. Firstly, we concatenate an auxiliary binary element to input vectors to indicate a missing input. The joint distribution of the time series is defined by first drawing a random permutation $o_d$ of time indices $1\dots T$ and then setting data points observed one by one in that order, starting from a fully missing sequence:
nodes.statement_short: Extend NADE to sequences: append a missingness indicator and define the joint law by revealing time steps in a random permutation order.
nodes.definiendum: The joint distribution of the time series
nodes.genus: a random permutation $o_d$ of time indices $1\dots T$
differentia: we concatenate an auxiliary binary element to input vectors to indicate a missing input
setting data points observed one by one in that order, starting from a fully missing sequence

nodes.name: NADE joint distribution of a time series
nodes.statement: \begin{align} P_{\mathrm{NADE}}(\mathbf{X}\mid o_d) = \prod_{d=1}^T P(\mathbf{x}_{o_d} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_{o_{e}}\}_{e=1}^{d-1}). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Given the permutation $o_d$, the sequence likelihood factorizes over time steps revealed in that order.

nodes.name: Filling in gaps in high-dimensional binary time series
nodes.statement: The task we aim to solve is to fill in gaps of multiple consecutive data points in high-dimensional binary time series data. The inference is not trivial for two reasons: firstly, we reconstruct multiple consecutive data points, which are likely to depend on each other, and secondly, we fill in data in the middle of a time series and hence need to consider the data both before and after the gap.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct several consecutive missing data points in the middle of a high-dimensional binary time series, using both past and future context.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: GSN approach to filling in gaps
nodes.statement: For filling in gaps with the GSN approach, we first train a bidirectional RNN to estimate $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$. In order to achieve that, we use the structure presented in Section~\ref{sec:bidirectional}. At test time, the gap is first initialized to random values, after which the missing values are sampled from the distribution $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ one by one in a random order repeatedly to approximate the stationary distribution. For the RNN structures used in this paper, the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+gM))$ where $d$ is the dimensionality of a data point, $c$ is the number of hidden units in the RNN, $T$ is the number of time steps in the data, $g$ is the length of the gap and $M$ is the number of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) steps used for inference.
nodes.statement_short: Train a BRNN for $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_t\mid\{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$, then Gibbs-resample the randomly initialized gap in random order until it mixes.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
input: a bidirectional RNN to estimate $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$
output: the missing values are sampled from the distribution $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ one by one in a random order repeatedly to approximate the stationary distribution

nodes.name: NADE approach to filling in gaps
nodes.statement: For filling in gaps with the NADE approach, we first train a bidirectional RNN where some of the inputs are set to a separate missing value token. At test time, all data points in the gap are first initialized with this token, after which each missing data point is reconstructed once until the whole gap is filled. Computationally, the main difference to GSN is that we do not have to sample each reconstructed data point multiple times, but the reconstruction is done in as many steps as there are missing data points in the gap. For the RNN structures used in this paper, the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+g))$ where $d$ is the dimensionality of a data point, $c$ is the number of hidden units in the RNN, $g$ is the length of the gap and $T$ is the number of time steps in the data.
nodes.statement_short: Train a BRNN with a missing-value token, then reconstruct each gap point exactly once instead of resampling it many times.

input: a bidirectional RNN where some of the inputs are set to a separate missing value token
output: each missing data point is reconstructed once until the whole gap is filled

nodes.name: Bayesian MCMC with a unidirectional RNN
nodes.statement: In addition to the two proposed methods, one can use a unidirectional RNN to solve the same task. We call this method \emph{Bayesian MCMC}. Using a unidirectional RNN for the task of filling in gaps is not trivial, as we need to take into account the probabilities of the values after the gap, which the model does not explicitly do. We therefore resort to a similar approach as the GSN approach, where we replace the $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ with a unidirectional equivalent for the Gibbs sampling. As the unidirectional RNN models conditional probabilities of the form $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1})$, we can use Bayes' theorem to derive:
nodes.statement_short: Gibbs sample the gap as in GSN, but obtain the leave-one-out conditional from a unidirectional RNN via Bayes' theorem.

output: the product of the outputs of the unidirectional RNN for time steps $t \ldots T$ for each possible $\mathbf{a}$

nodes.name: Adopt a unidirectional RNN as the sampler
nodes.statement: In addition to the two proposed methods, one can use a unidirectional RNN to solve the same task. We call this method \emph{Bayesian MCMC}.
nodes.statement_short: Name the unidirectional-RNN variant of the gap-filling task Bayesian MCMC.

nodes.statement: We therefore resort to a similar approach as the GSN approach, where we replace the $P_{\mathrm{BRNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{t} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ with a unidirectional equivalent for the Gibbs sampling.
nodes.statement_short: Reuse the GSN Gibbs loop but swap in a unidirectional conditional.

nodes.statement: As the unidirectional RNN models conditional probabilities of the form $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1})$, we can use Bayes' theorem to derive:
nodes.statement_short: Turn one-step-ahead conditionals into the leave-one-out conditional via Bayes' theorem.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: Bayes derivation of the unidirectional leave-one-out conditional
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \hspace{2em}&\hspace{-2em} P_{\mathrm{RNN}}\left( \mathbf{x}_{t} = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_{d}\}_{d\neq t} \right) \\ & \propto P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left( \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} \right) P_{\mathrm{RNN}} \left(\{\mathbf{x}_e\}_{e=t+1}^{T} \mid \mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{a}, \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{t-1} \right) \\ &= \prod_{\tau=t}^T P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_{\tau} \mid \{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d=1}^{\tau-1}) \Bigr|_{\mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{a}} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $P_{\mathrm{RNN}}(\mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{a}\mid\{\mathbf{x}_d\}_{d\neq t})$ is proportional to the product of the RNN outputs from $t$ to $T$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{a}$.

nodes.name: Feasibility and cost of Bayesian MCMC inference
nodes.statement: In some cases this is feasible to evaluate. For categorical data, e.g. text, there are as many possible values for $\mathbf{a}$ as there are dimensions\footnote{For character-based text, the number of dimensions is the number of characters in the model alphabet.}. However, for other binary data the number of possibilities grows exponentially, and is clearly not feasible to evaluate. For the RNN structures used in this paper, the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+aTM))$ where $a$ is the number of different values a data point can have, $d$ is the dimensionality of a data point, $c$ is the number of hidden units in the RNN, $T$ is the number of time steps in the data, and $M$ is the number of MCMC steps used for inference. The critical difference in complexity to the GSN approach is the coefficient $a$, that for categorical data takes the value $d$, for binary vectors $2^d$ and for continuous data is infinite.
nodes.statement_short: Enumerating proposals $\mathbf{a}$ is feasible for categorical data but grows as $2^d$ for binary vectors and is infinite for continuous data.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
conclusions: there are as many possible values for $\mathbf{a}$ as there are dimensions
the number of possibilities grows exponentially, and is clearly not feasible to evaluate
the computational complexity of this approach at test time is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)(T+aTM))$

nodes.name: One-gram baseline model
nodes.statement: As a simple baseline model, we also evaluate the \emph{one-gram} log-likelihood of the gaps. The one-gram model assumes a constant context-independent categorical distribution for the categorical task, or a vector of factorial binomial probabilities for the structured prediction task:
nodes.statement_short: A context-independent baseline: one fixed categorical (or factorial binomial) distribution for every time step.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
differentia: a constant context-independent categorical distribution for the categorical task, or a vector of factorial binomial probabilities for the structured prediction task

nodes.name: One-gram predictive distribution
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} P_{\mathrm{one-gram}}\left(\mathbf{y}_t \right) = \mathrm{f} \left( \mathbf{b}_y \right). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The one-gram prediction depends only on the output bias $\mathbf{b}_y$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks

nodes.name: One-way inference
nodes.statement: We also compare to \emph{one-way inference}, where the data points in the gap are reconstructed in order without taking the future context into account, using Equations (\ref{eq:uni_y}) and (\ref{eq:uni_h}) directly. The computational complexity is $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)T)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct the gap left-to-right with the unidirectional RNN equations, ignoring future context, in $\mathcal{O}((dc+c^2)T)$.
nodes.section: 4 Filling in gaps with Recurrent Neural Networks
output: the data points in the gap are reconstructed in order without taking the future context into account

nodes.name: Two experimental settings
nodes.statement: We run two sets of experiments: one for a categorical prediction task, and one for a binary structured prediction task. In the categorical prediction task we fill in gaps of five characters in Wikipedia text, while in the structural prediction task we fill in gaps of five time steps in different polyphonic music data sets.
nodes.statement_short: Two tasks: five-character gaps in Wikipedia text, and five-time-step gaps in polyphonic music.

nodes.name: Training procedure for the categorical prediction task
nodes.statement: For the categorical prediction task, we test the performance of the two proposed methods, GSN and NADE. In addition, we compare the performance to MCMC using Bayesian inference and one-way inference with a unidirectional RNN. We therefore have to train three different RNNs, one for each method. Each RNN is trained as a predictor network, where the character at each step is predicted based on all the previous characters (in the case of the RNN) or all the previous and following characters (in the case of the BRNNs). We use the same data set as \citet{sutskever2011generating}, which consists of 2GB of English text from Wikipedia. For training, we follow a similar strategy as \citet{NIPS2013_5166}. The characters are encoded as one-hot binary vectors with a dimensionality of $d=96$ characters and the output is modelled with a softmax distribution. We train the unirectional RNN with string lengths of $T=250$ characters, where the error is propagated only from the last 200 outputs. In the BRNN we use string length of $T=300$ characters, where the error is propagated from the middle 200 outputs. We therefore avoid propagating the gradient from predictions that lack long temporal context. For the BRNN used in the NADE method, we add one dimension to the one-hot input which corresponds to a missing value token. During training, in each minibatch we mark $g=5$ consecutive characters every 25 time steps as a gap. During training, the error is propagated only from these gaps. For each gap, we uniformly draw a value from 1 to 5, and set that many characters in the gap to the missing value token. The model is therefore trained to predict the output in different stages of inference, where a number of the inputs are still marked as missing. For comparison, we also train a similar network, but without masking. In that variant, the error is therefore propagated from all time steps. We refer to ``NADE'' masked and ``NADE no mask'', respectively, for these two training methods. For all the models, the weight elements are drawn from the uniform distribution: $w_{i,j}\sim \mathcal{U}\left[-s, s\right]$ where $s=1$ for the input to hidden layer, and following \citet{glorot2010understanding}, where $s=\sqrt{6/\left(d_{in} + d_{out}\right)}$ for the hidden-to-hidden and the hidden-to output layers. The biases are initialized to zero. We use $c=1000$ hidden units in the unidirectional RNN and $c=684$ hidden units in the two hidden layers in the BRNNs. The number of parameters in the two model types is therefore roughly the same. In the recurrent layers, we set the recurrent activation connected to the first time step to zero. The networks are trained using stochastic gradient descent and the gradient is calculated using backpropagation through time. We use a minibatch size of 40, i.e. each minibatch consists of 40 randomly sampled sequences of length 250. As the gradients tend to occasionally ``blow up'' when training RNNs \citep{bengio1994learning,pascanu2013difficulty}, we normalize the gradients at each update to have length one. The step size is set to 0.25 for all layers in the beginning of training, and it is linearly decayed to zero during training. As training the model is very time-consuming\footnote{We used about 8 weeks of GPU time for the reported results.}, we do not optimize the hyperparameters, or repeat runs to get confidence intervals around the evaluated performances.
nodes.statement_short: Train three character-level networks (RNN, BRNN, masked-NADE BRNN) on Wikipedia text with SGD, normalized gradients and a linearly decayed step size.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task
output: three different RNNs, one for each method

nodes.name: Decide which models to train
nodes.statement: For the categorical prediction task, we test the performance of the two proposed methods, GSN and NADE. In addition, we compare the performance to MCMC using Bayesian inference and one-way inference with a unidirectional RNN. We therefore have to train three different RNNs, one for each method.
nodes.statement_short: Three networks are needed: GSN, NADE and the unidirectional baseline.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task

nodes.name: Train each network as a next-character predictor
nodes.statement: Each RNN is trained as a predictor network, where the character at each step is predicted based on all the previous characters (in the case of the RNN) or all the previous and following characters (in the case of the BRNNs).
nodes.statement_short: Each network predicts the current character from the preceding (RNN) or surrounding (BRNN) characters.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task

nodes.name: Set up the Wikipedia data and sequence lengths
nodes.statement: We use the same data set as \citet{sutskever2011generating}, which consists of 2GB of English text from Wikipedia. For training, we follow a similar strategy as \citet{NIPS2013_5166}. The characters are encoded as one-hot binary vectors with a dimensionality of $d=96$ characters and the output is modelled with a softmax distribution. We train the unirectional RNN with string lengths of $T=250$ characters, where the error is propagated only from the last 200 outputs. In the BRNN we use string length of $T=300$ characters, where the error is propagated from the middle 200 outputs. We therefore avoid propagating the gradient from predictions that lack long temporal context.
nodes.statement_short: Use 2GB of Wikipedia text, $d=96$ one-hot characters, and propagate error only from the central/last 200 outputs.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task

nodes.name: Add and randomize the missing value token for NADE
nodes.statement: For the BRNN used in the NADE method, we add one dimension to the one-hot input which corresponds to a missing value token. During training, in each minibatch we mark $g=5$ consecutive characters every 25 time steps as a gap. During training, the error is propagated only from these gaps. For each gap, we uniformly draw a value from 1 to 5, and set that many characters in the gap to the missing value token. The model is therefore trained to predict the output in different stages of inference, where a number of the inputs are still marked as missing. For comparison, we also train a similar network, but without masking. In that variant, the error is therefore propagated from all time steps. We refer to ``NADE'' masked and ``NADE no mask'', respectively, for these two training methods.
nodes.statement_short: Mark $g=5$ characters every 25 steps as a gap and randomly hide 1-5 of them, giving the ``NADE masked'' and ``NADE no mask'' variants.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task

nodes.name: Initialize the weights and biases
nodes.statement: For all the models, the weight elements are drawn from the uniform distribution: $w_{i,j}\sim \mathcal{U}\left[-s, s\right]$ where $s=1$ for the input to hidden layer, and following \citet{glorot2010understanding}, where $s=\sqrt{6/\left(d_{in} + d_{out}\right)}$ for the hidden-to-hidden and the hidden-to output layers. The biases are initialized to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform weight initialization with Glorot scaling for hidden layers; zero biases.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task

nodes.name: Match the parameter counts of RNN and BRNN
nodes.statement: We use $c=1000$ hidden units in the unidirectional RNN and $c=684$ hidden units in the two hidden layers in the BRNNs. The number of parameters in the two model types is therefore roughly the same. In the recurrent layers, we set the recurrent activation connected to the first time step to zero.
nodes.statement_short: $c=1000$ hidden units in the RNN vs $c=684$ in each BRNN layer, so both models have roughly equal parameter counts.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task

nodes.name: Optimize by SGD with normalized gradients
nodes.statement: The networks are trained using stochastic gradient descent and the gradient is calculated using backpropagation through time. We use a minibatch size of 40, i.e. each minibatch consists of 40 randomly sampled sequences of length 250. As the gradients tend to occasionally ``blow up'' when training RNNs \citep{bengio1994learning,pascanu2013difficulty}, we normalize the gradients at each update to have length one. The step size is set to 0.25 for all layers in the beginning of training, and it is linearly decayed to zero during training. As training the model is very time-consuming\footnote{We used about 8 weeks of GPU time for the reported results.}, we do not optimize the hyperparameters, or repeat runs to get confidence intervals around the evaluated performances.
nodes.statement_short: Backpropagation through time, minibatch 40, gradients normalized to unit length, step size 0.25 decayed linearly to zero.
nodes.section: 5.1 Training details for categorical prediction task

nodes.name: Training procedure for the binary structured prediction task
nodes.statement: In the other set of experiments, we use four polyphonic music data sets \citep{boulanger2012modeling}. The data sets consist of at least 7 hours of polyphonic music each, where each data point is a binary $d=88$-dimensional vector that represents one time step of MIDI-encoded music, indicating which of the 88 keys of a piano are pressed. We test the performance of the two proposed methods, but omit training the unidirectional RNNs as the computational complexity of the Bayesian MCMC is prohibitive ($a=2^{88}$). We train all models for $50~000$ updates in minibatches of $\approx 3~000$ individual data points\footnote{A minibatch can therefore consist of e.g. $100$ musical scores, each of length $T=30$.}. As the data sets are small, we select the initial learning rate on a grid of $\left\lbrace 0.0001, 0.0003, \ldots, 0.3, 1\right\rbrace$ based on the lowest validation set cost. We use no ``burn-in'' as several of the scores are fairly short, and therefore do not specifically mask out values in the beginning or end of the data set as we did for the text data. For the NADE method, we use an additional dimension as a missing value token in the data. For the missing values, we set the missing value token to one and the other dimensions to zero. Other training details are similar to the categorical prediction task.
nodes.statement_short: Train the two proposed BRNN models on four polyphonic music sets for 50 000 updates, selecting the learning rate on a grid by validation cost.
nodes.section: 5.2 Training Details for the Binary Structured Prediction Task
output: We test the performance of the two proposed methods

nodes.name: Set up the polyphonic music data
nodes.statement: In the other set of experiments, we use four polyphonic music data sets \citep{boulanger2012modeling}. The data sets consist of at least 7 hours of polyphonic music each, where each data point is a binary $d=88$-dimensional vector that represents one time step of MIDI-encoded music, indicating which of the 88 keys of a piano are pressed.
nodes.statement_short: Four polyphonic music sets of binary $d=88$-dimensional MIDI vectors, at least 7 hours each.
nodes.section: 5.2 Training Details for the Binary Structured Prediction Task

nodes.name: Omit the unidirectional Bayesian MCMC model
nodes.statement: We test the performance of the two proposed methods, but omit training the unidirectional RNNs as the computational complexity of the Bayesian MCMC is prohibitive ($a=2^{88}$).
nodes.statement_short: Skip Bayesian MCMC here because $a=2^{88}$ makes it intractable.
nodes.section: 5.2 Training Details for the Binary Structured Prediction Task

nodes.name: Run the updates and select the learning rate
nodes.statement: We train all models for $50~000$ updates in minibatches of $\approx 3~000$ individual data points\footnote{A minibatch can therefore consist of e.g. $100$ musical scores, each of length $T=30$.}. As the data sets are small, we select the initial learning rate on a grid of $\left\lbrace 0.0001, 0.0003, \ldots, 0.3, 1\right\rbrace$ based on the lowest validation set cost. We use no ``burn-in'' as several of the scores are fairly short, and therefore do not specifically mask out values in the beginning or end of the data set as we did for the text data.
nodes.statement_short: 50 000 updates on ~3 000-point minibatches, learning rate chosen on a grid by validation cost, no burn-in masking.
nodes.section: 5.2 Training Details for the Binary Structured Prediction Task

nodes.name: Encode the missing value token for NADE
nodes.statement: For the NADE method, we use an additional dimension as a missing value token in the data. For the missing values, we set the missing value token to one and the other dimensions to zero.
nodes.statement_short: An extra input dimension flags missing music time steps.
nodes.section: 5.2 Training Details for the Binary Structured Prediction Task

nodes.name: Gap log-likelihood evaluation criterion
nodes.statement: At test time, we evaluate the models by calculating the mean log-likelihood of the correct value of gaps of five consecutive missing values in test data.
nodes.definiendum: the mean log-likelihood of the correct value of gaps of five consecutive missing values in test data

nodes.name: Evaluation of GSN and Bayesian MCMC by Gibbs sampling
nodes.statement: In the GSN and Bayesian MCMC approaches, we first set the five values in the gap to a random value for the categorical prediction task, or to zero for the structured prediction task. We then sample all five values in the gap in random order, and repeat the procedure for $M=100$ MCMC steps\footnote{$M=100$ MCMC steps means that each value in the gap of $g=5$ will be resampled $M/g=20$ times}. For evaluating the log-likelihood of the correct value for the string, we force the last five steps to sample the correct value, and store the probability of the model sampling those values. We also evaluate the probability of reconstructing correctly the individual data points by not forcing the last five time steps to sample the correct value, but by storing the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately. We run the MCMC chain 100 times and use the log of the mean of the likelihoods of predicting the correct value over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: Initialize the gap, run $M=100$ MCMC steps, force the last five samples to the correct value, and average likelihoods over 100 chains.

nodes.name: Initialize the gap values
nodes.statement: In the GSN and Bayesian MCMC approaches, we first set the five values in the gap to a random value for the categorical prediction task, or to zero for the structured prediction task.
nodes.statement_short: Start from random values (text) or zeros (music).

nodes.name: Run the MCMC chain
nodes.statement: We then sample all five values in the gap in random order, and repeat the procedure for $M=100$ MCMC steps\footnote{$M=100$ MCMC steps means that each value in the gap of $g=5$ will be resampled $M/g=20$ times}.
nodes.statement_short: Resample all five gap values in random order for $M=100$ MCMC steps.

nodes.name: Force the correct value to score the whole gap
nodes.statement: For evaluating the log-likelihood of the correct value for the string, we force the last five steps to sample the correct value, and store the probability of the model sampling those values.
nodes.statement_short: Clamp the final five samples to the truth and record their probability.

nodes.name: Score individual data points without forcing
nodes.statement: We also evaluate the probability of reconstructing correctly the individual data points by not forcing the last five time steps to sample the correct value, but by storing the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately.
nodes.statement_short: For per-point scores, record reconstruction probabilities without clamping.

nodes.name: Average over 100 chains
nodes.statement: We run the MCMC chain 100 times and use the log of the mean of the likelihoods of predicting the correct value over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: Report the log of the mean likelihood across 100 independent chains.

nodes.name: Evaluation of one-directional inference
nodes.statement: When evaluating the performance of one-directional inference, we use a similar approach to MCMC. However, when evaluating the log-likelihood of the entire gap, we only construct it once in sequential order, and record the probabilities of reconstructing the correct value. When evaluating the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately, we use the same approach as for MCMC and sample the gap 100 times, recording for each step the probability of sampling the correct value. The result for each data point is the log of the mean of the likelihoods over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: Score the gap by a single sequential reconstruction, and per-point scores by averaging 100 sampled gaps.

nodes.name: Reuse the MCMC evaluation protocol
nodes.statement: When evaluating the performance of one-directional inference, we use a similar approach to MCMC.
nodes.statement_short: Follow the MCMC evaluation protocol as a starting point.

nodes.name: Construct the gap once in sequential order
nodes.statement: However, when evaluating the log-likelihood of the entire gap, we only construct it once in sequential order, and record the probabilities of reconstructing the correct value.
nodes.statement_short: Build the whole gap in one left-to-right pass and record its probability.

nodes.name: Average per-point probabilities over 100 samples
nodes.statement: When evaluating the probability of reconstructing the correct value for each data point separately, we use the same approach as for MCMC and sample the gap 100 times, recording for each step the probability of sampling the correct value. The result for each data point is the log of the mean of the likelihoods over these 100 runs.
nodes.statement_short: For per-point scores, sample the gap 100 times and take the log of the mean likelihood.

nodes.name: Test set sizes used for evaluation
nodes.statement: On the Wikipedia data, we evaluate the GSN and NADE methods on 50~000 gaps on the test data. On the music data, all models are evaluated on all possible gaps of $g=5$ on the test data, excluding gaps that intersect with the first and last 10 time steps of a score. When evaluating the Bayesian MCMC with the unidirectional RNN, we have to significantly limit the size of the data set, as the method is highly computationally complex. We therefore run it on 1~000 gaps on the test data.
nodes.statement_short: 50 000 Wikipedia gaps, all admissible music gaps, but only 1 000 gaps for the expensive Bayesian MCMC.

nodes.name: Exact NADE evaluation over all reconstruction orders
nodes.statement: For NADE, we set the five time steps in the gap to the missing value token. We then reconstruct them one by one to the correct value, and record the probability of the correct reconstruction. We repeat this process for all possible permutations of the order in which to do the reconstruction, and therefore acquire the exact probability of the correct reconstruction given the model and the data. We also evaluate the individual character reconstruction probabilities by recording the probability of sampling the correct value given all other values in the gap are set to missing.
nodes.statement_short: Reconstruct the gap in every permutation order to obtain the exact probability of the correct reconstruction.

nodes.name: Mark the gap as missing
nodes.statement: For NADE, we set the five time steps in the gap to the missing value token.
nodes.statement_short: Set all five gap steps to the missing-value token.

nodes.name: Reconstruct to the correct value one by one
nodes.statement: We then reconstruct them one by one to the correct value, and record the probability of the correct reconstruction.
nodes.statement_short: Reveal the true values one at a time, recording each reconstruction probability.

nodes.name: Average over all permutations for the exact probability
nodes.statement: We repeat this process for all possible permutations of the order in which to do the reconstruction, and therefore acquire the exact probability of the correct reconstruction given the model and the data.
nodes.statement_short: Enumerating all orders yields the exact reconstruction probability.

nodes.name: Score individual characters from the fully missing gap
nodes.statement: We also evaluate the individual character reconstruction probabilities by recording the probability of sampling the correct value given all other values in the gap are set to missing.
nodes.statement_short: Per-character scores condition on all other gap values being missing.

nodes.name: Bayesian MCMC yields the best gap NLL, GSN and NADE beat one-way inference
nodes.statement: From Table~\ref{tab:bps} we can see that the Bayesian MCMC method seems to yield the best results, while GSN or NADE outperform one-way inference. It is worth noting that in the most difficult data sets, piano and JSB, oneway inference performs very well.
nodes.statement_short: Bayesian MCMC is best where feasible, GSN and NADE beat one-way inference, except on the hardest sets (Piano, JSB).
conclusions: the Bayesian MCMC method seems to yield the best results, while GSN or NADE outperform one-way inference
in the most difficult data sets, piano and JSB, oneway inference performs very well

nodes.name: GSN performance saturates with the number of MCMC steps
nodes.statement: In order to get an indication of how the number of MCMC steps in the GSN approach affects performance, we plotted the difference in NLL of GSN and NADE of the test set as a function of the number of MCMC steps in Figure~\ref{fig:mcmc_iters} (supplementary material). The figure indicates that the music data sets mix fairly well, as the performance of GSN quickly saturates. However, for the Wikipedia data, the performance could probably be even further improved by letting the MCMC chain run for more than $M=100$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: Music data mix quickly so GSN saturates fast, while Wikipedia would still improve beyond $M=100$ MCMC steps.
assumptions: we plotted the difference in NLL of GSN and NADE of the test set as a function of the number of MCMC steps
conclusions: the music data sets mix fairly well, as the performance of GSN quickly saturates
for the Wikipedia data, the performance could probably be even further improved by letting the MCMC chain run for more than $M=100$ steps

nodes.name: Positions near the gap edges are easiest to predict
nodes.statement: In Figure~\ref{fig:chars} we have evaluated the NLL for the individual characters in the gaps of length five. As expected, all methods except for one-way inference are better at predicting characters close to both edges of the gap.
nodes.statement_short: Every method except one-way inference predicts the gap's edge positions better than its middle.
assumptions: In Figure~\ref{fig:chars} we have evaluated the NLL for the individual characters in the gaps of length five
conclusions: all methods except for one-way inference are better at predicting characters close to both edges of the gap

nodes.name: Sanity check: the BRNNs are trained successfully
nodes.statement: As a sanity check, we make sure our models have been successfully trained by evaluating the mean test log-likelihood of the BRNNs for gap sizes of one. In Table~\ref{tab:nll_train} (supplementary material) we can see that the BRNNs expectedly outperform previously published results with unidirectional RNNs, which indicates that the models have been trained successfully.
nodes.statement_short: On gap size one the BRNNs beat published unidirectional RNN numbers, confirming successful training.
assumptions: evaluating the mean test log-likelihood of the BRNNs for gap sizes of one
conclusions: the BRNNs expectedly outperform previously published results with unidirectional RNNs
which indicates that the models have been trained successfully

nodes.name: Summary of the proposed approach
nodes.statement: Although recurrent neural networks have been used as generative models for time series data, it has not been trivial how to use them for inference in cases such as missing gaps in the sequential data. In this paper, we proposed to use bidirectional RNNs as generative models for time series, with two probabilistic interpretations called GSN and NADE. Both provide efficient inference in both positive and negative directions in time, and both can be used in tasks where Bayesian inference of a unidirectional RNN is computationally infeasible.
nodes.statement_short: BRNNs with the GSN and NADE interpretations give efficient bidirectional inference where Bayesian inference on a unidirectional RNN is infeasible.

nodes.name: Three ways the NADE model differed from the basic BRNN
nodes.statement: The model we trained for NADE differed from the basic BRNN in several ways: Firstly, we artificially marked gaps of 5 consecutive points as missing, which should help in specializing the model for such reconstruction tasks. It would be interesting to study the effect of the missingness pattern used in training, on the learned representations and predictions. Secondly, in addition to using all outputs as the training signal, we tested using only the reconstructions of those missing values as the training signal. This reduces the effective amount of training that the model went through. Thirdly, the model had one more input (the missingness indicator) that makes the learning task more difficult.
nodes.statement_short: NADE differed by artificial 5-point gaps, by training only on reconstructions, and by the extra missingness-indicator input.

nodes.name: Effect of the training missingness pattern
nodes.statement: It would be interesting to study the effect of the missingness pattern used in training, on the learned representations and predictions.

nodes.name: Training differences degrade the NADE model's single-value reconstruction
nodes.statement: We can see from Table~\ref{tab:nll_train} that the model we trained for NADE where we only used the reconstructions as the training signal has a worse performance than the BRNN for reconstructing single values. This indicates that these differences in training have a significant impact on the quality of the final trained probabilistic model.
nodes.statement_short: Training only on reconstructions costs single-value accuracy relative to the BRNN, so these training choices matter.
assumptions: the model we trained for NADE where we only used the reconstructions as the training signal
conclusions: has a worse performance than the BRNN for reconstructing single values
these differences in training have a significant impact on the quality of the final trained probabilistic model

nodes.name: Optimal allocation of parameters between RNN and BRNN
nodes.statement: We used the same number of parameters when training an RNN and a BRNN. The RNN can concentrate all the learning effort on forward prediction, and re-use the learned dependencies in backward inference by the computationally heavy Bayesian inference. It remains an open question which approach would work best given an optimal size of the hidden layers.
nodes.statement_short: With optimally sized hidden layers, it is unknown whether the unidirectional or the bidirectional approach wins.

nodes.name: Future work on model structure
nodes.statement: As future work, other model structures could be explored in this context, for instance the Long Short-Term Memory \citep{hochreiter1997long}. Specifically to our NADE approach, it might make sense to replace the regular additive connection from the missingness indicator input to the hidden activations in Eq.~(\ref{eq:bi_hf},\ref{eq:bi_hb}), by a multiplicative connection that somehow gates the dynamics mappings $\mathbf{W}_h^f$ and $\mathbf{W}_h^b$. Another direction to extend is to use a deep architecture with more hidden layers.
nodes.statement_short: Suggests LSTM units, a multiplicative gate for the missingness indicator, and deeper architectures.

nodes.name: Structured prediction and stochastic hidden units
nodes.statement: The midi music data is an example of a structured prediction task: Components of the output vector depend strongly on each other. However, our model assumes independent Bernoulli distributions for them. One way to take those dependencies into account is to use stochastic hidden units $\mathbf{h}_t^f$ and $\mathbf{h}_t^b$, which has been shown to improve performance on structured prediction tasks \citep{Raiko2015techniques}. \citet{bayer2014learning} explored that approach, and reconstructed missing values in the middle of motion capture data. In their reconstruction method, the hidden stochastic variables are selected based on an auxiliary inference model, after which the missing values are reconstructed conditioned on the hidden stochastic variable values. Both steps are done with maximum a posteriori point selection instead of sampling. Further quantitative evaluation of the method would be an interesting point of comparison.
nodes.statement_short: The independent-Bernoulli output ignores component dependencies; stochastic hidden units, as used by Bayer & Osendorfer, could capture them.

nodes.name: Extension to continuous-valued data
nodes.statement: The proposed methods could be easily extended to continuous-valued data. As an example application, time-series reconstructions with a recurrent model has been shown to be effective in speech recognition especially under impulsive noise \citep{remes2011missing}.
nodes.statement_short: The methods should carry over to continuous data, e.g. speech reconstruction under impulsive noise.
